instruction.text: Read the description of George Orwell's novel 1984.

atoms.text:
1984 is a dystopian novel set in the totalitarian state of Oceania, where the Party controls every aspect of people's lives through surveillance, propaganda and censorship. Using Newspeak, a language designed to limit vocabulary and independent thought, the Party prevents people from thinking freely, destroying individuality.
The novel follows Winston Smith, who secretly rebels against the regime and begins a forbidden relationship with Julia. Romantic relationships are forbidden because the Party wants people's loyalty to belong only to the state, not to another person. After being arrested, Winston is tortured until he abandons his beliefs and accepts the Party's ideology.

instruction.text: Decide whether the statements are true or false.

atoms.a: At the end of the novel, Winston remains loyal to his own beliefs despite being imprisoned.
The purpose of Newspeak is to restrict people's ability to think critically and individually.

Which dystopian themes does the novel address?

b: ++It is a totalitarian state where the Party controls people's actions, thoughts, and access to information.

instruction.text: Read the excerpt from chapter one of 1984 and fill in the gaps below.

atoms.text: “The telescreen received and transmitted simultaneously. Any sound that Winston made, above the level of a very low whisper, would be picked up by it; moreover, so long as he remained within the field of vision [...], he could be seen as well as heard. There was of course no way of knowing whether you were being watched at any given moment.”

atoms.b: The author presents technology as a ((tool_of_control)) rather than ((entertainment)).
This quotation shows how a dystopian government controls its citizens through ((surveillance_and_fear)) instead of relying only on physical ((violence --freedom)).

instruction.text: Read the excerpt from chapter seven of 1984 and fill in the gaps below.

atoms.text:
“If they could make me stop loving you—that would be the real betrayal,’ [said Winston].
[Julia] thought it over. ‘They can’t do that... They can make you say anything—anything—but they can’t make you believe it. They can’t get inside you.”

atoms.b: In this dialogue, the author explores the ((conflict)) between the individual and the state.
Winston fears that the Party could destroy his ((identity)), while ((Julia)) argues that people's thoughts will always remain independent.
The quotation questions whether a government can control not only people's ((behaviour)), but also their private emotions as ((individuals)).
At the end of the novel, Winston is tortured until he ((betrays --loves)) Julia and his beliefs, fully supporting the regime's ideology.

atoms.b: In this quotation, Syme, who is an expert in Newspeak, explains that the Party uses ((language)) to limit thought.
By reducing people's vocabulary, it also reduces their ability to express ideas that are ((dangerous)) for the government. As a result, ((independent)) thinking becomes ((impossible)).
The author suggests that those in power can shape reality by determining which words and ideas are ((available --reliable)).
